source.title: Charting 15 Years of Progress in Deep Learning for Speech Emotion Recognition: A Replication Study
source.authors: Andreas Triantafyllopoulos; A. Batliner; Björn W. Schuller

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the scaling hypothesis and reports model-size associations for speech-emotion-recognition systems, but it does not test language-model pretraining loss laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its audio-model results are a different system type from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports correlations between audio-model complexity and downstream SER performance. These are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the language-model claim. It also discusses scaling in SER, but does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or sweep compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: This is a speech-emotion-recognition benchmarking study. Its 'scaling' results are Spearman correlations between downstream UAR and parameter count or MACs across 43 heterogeneous audio architectures, trained with fixed hyperparameters. It fits no power law, measures no pretraining loss, and varies no size, data or compute within one model family. The authors note the scaling hypothesis is 'typically applied within the same architecture family' and say they could not test that. The cross-architecture correlations therefore do not measure what V5 or V6 name (predictable improvement with scale under a common recipe). They are recorded as related findings, not as tests. The paper cites Kaplan et al. and urges caution about the scaling hypothesis without giving a version-specific argument.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. In fuller form: results point to diminishing returns and a plateau after transformers were introduced. Bigger and newer models did not reliably give better in-domain or out-of-domain performance, robustness or fairness. Conclusions depend on which models are selected and on hyperparameter tuning, so the answer is called inconclusive. The authors say their cross-architecture comparison does not test within-family scaling, and they urge caution about the scaling hypothesis, including because of publication bias.
record.recipe_differences: This is a speech-emotion-recognition benchmarking and replication study, not a language-model scaling-law experiment. It compares SER architectures across datasets and reports downstream classification metrics rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Model rankings and performance varied substantially with hyperparameter choices; the paper also notes that conclusions about progress depend on which models are selected.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 43 heterogeneous audio SER architectures (exploration phase, fixed hyperparameters), Spearman's ρ between in-domain UAR and MACs or parameter count ranged from -.083 to .230. All bootstrap 95% CIs include zero (Table II).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across architecturally diverse SER models trained with a shared fixed recipe, model size or compute does not consistently predict downstream SER accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Correlations of model size or MACs with out-of-domain UAR (EmoDB, IEMOCAP: .064–.172) and with 0 dB noisy-audio UAR (.03–.10) were low. Clean and noisy UAR correlated at .953.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across diverse SER architectures, size does not predict out-of-domain generalisation or noise robustness.

record.problems: The authors report limited datasets, model coverage, compute, and hyperparameter tuning, and state that model selection and tuning choices make outcomes inconclusive. The size-performance results are correlations across selected SER architectures, not controlled scaling runs; some reported correlations have broad confidence intervals including zero.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were omitted. Results for year of publication, fairness, and other non-performance measures were not included because they do not measure the scaling behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss curves or power-law fits.
Extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
Shape effects at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in audio or fine-tuning regimes. No within-family size sweep or power-law fit was done.
Downstream performance versus scale within a model family or versus pretraining loss. Only cross-architecture correlations of SER UAR with parameters and MACs are reported.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices. The paper shows hyperparameters change SER model rankings, but no scaling-law fits are made.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are kept. The rows are cross-architecture correlations, not controlled scaling runs, and are correctly linked to none. The record correctly omits correlations of year with performance and of the Gini fairness index with size; they are not loss or performance scaling. The text-based models (BERT-base vs 7B LLMs) are also not a controlled scaling comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Architecture-shape effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of language-model downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss. The paper evaluates SER systems, not language-model scaling.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices or setup.
